bullets: How to place any probability on the scale from 0 to 1, write it as a fraction, decimal or percentage, and multiply along the branches for combined events
slides.heading: E-Math probability: single and combined events
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we build probability from one fair coin and one bag of counters, all the way to two tosses at once.

bullets: Calculate the probability of a single event as favourable outcomes over total outcomes
Combine independent events by multiplying along the branches of a possibility table
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the goals aloud and tell the class: keep these in mind, because the exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things.

bullets: A coin has just landed heads three times in a row - what is the chance the next toss is tails?
Is it more than a half, less than a half, or exactly a half?
slides.heading: Three heads in a row - is tails due?
slides.notes: Ask for predictions and take two or three answers without judging them yet; say: the last scene puts this exact claim on trial.

bullets: Every probability sits between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain), and can be written as a fraction, a decimal or a percentage
P(event) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes, and for independent combined events the probabilities multiply
slides.heading: One scale, one fraction, one product
slides.notes: Say this slowly, because it is the map for the whole lesson: first the scale, then the fraction, then the product for two events together.

bullets: The marker slides along the scale from 0, impossible, through 1/2, an even chance, to 1, certain
Every probability in this lesson will land somewhere on this one line
slides.heading: The probability scale
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: follow the marker as it travels the scale and name each stop as it arrives.

bullets: The same probability wears three outfits: the fraction 1/2, the decimal 0.5 and 50%
A fair coin landing heads is all three at once
slides.heading: One value, three forms
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: one value stays fixed while its three written forms appear around it.

bullets: Five outcomes, three of them favourable: the three gold dots gather into the favourable chip
All five gather into the total chip, and the probability builds as 3/5
slides.heading: P(event) = favourable ÷ total
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: count the dots into the favourable chip first, then into the total chip, and watch the fraction assemble.

bullets: Toss a coin twice and the grid draws itself: four cells, one per outcome
Four dots travel in - heads-heads, heads-tails, tails-heads, tails-tails - each label arriving with its dot
slides.heading: Two tosses, one table
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: each dot flies to its own cell, so the whole sample space is visible at once.

bullets: Each of the four outcomes is equally likely, so each cell carries probability 1/4
Heads-then-heads is 1/2 times 1/2, which is 1/4 - multiply along the branches
slides.heading: Fill the table, multiply the branches
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: the branches fill with halves and their product lands in the heads-heads cell.

bullets: Three heads land in a row, and tails starts to feel overdue
The coin remembers nothing: the next toss is still heads or tails, 1/2 each
slides.heading: The gambler's slip: coins have no memory
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: the streak builds, the feeling builds with it, and then the fresh coin resets everything to an even chance.

bullets: A bag holds 5 counters, 3 of them red: P(red) = favourable / total = 3/5
As a decimal that is 0.6, and as a percentage 60%
slides.heading: Worked example: three red counters out of five
slides.notes: Work this on the board slowly: count the favourable counters, count them all, divide - then convert the one answer into its other two forms.

bullets: A bag holds 4 blue counters and 6 green counters - find P(blue) as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage
Then open the worksheet: one scale question, one three-forms question and one two-toss table
slides.heading: Your turn
slides.notes: Give three quiet minutes for the first task, take the three forms from the class, then set the worksheet going in pairs.

bullets: Four questions: the next toss after a streak, a favourable-over-total fraction, one cell of the two-toss table, and a branch product
Write one sentence: why does a run of heads change nothing about the next toss?
slides.heading: Exit ticket
slides.notes: Collect the tickets at the door; the first question revisits the trap from the last scene, so it shows straight away who trusts the coin's short memory.
